::: {.callout-tip}
## One coherent example

We use six invented shop orders with **distance (km)**, **number of items**, and **fulfilment time (minutes)**. Start the [single-file Python example](../../examples/README.md); this chapter corresponds to `python3 delivery_ml_lab.py probability`.
:::

## The motivating problem

**How should a predictor express what it does not know?**

Probability spaces specify events, distributions specify uncertain quantities, Bayes' rule updates beliefs, and Gaussian models provide a tractable noise assumption. Conjugate priors and variable transformations show that uncertainty can be manipulated mathematically.

## Central mathematical relationship

$$
p(\theta\mid D)\propto p(D\mid\theta)p(\theta)
$$

The equation captures the chapter's principal relationship. Definitions and assumptions are developed in the lessons below; an equation is useful only when the domain and meaning of its symbols are explicit.

## First worked result

Of our six invented orders, three take at least 16 minutes. The empirical late fraction is 3/6. This is a property of the observed sample, not a guarantee about the next order; a probabilistic model can express that uncertainty.

## What to pay attention to

A density is not itself a point probability. Independence of random variables differs from linear independence of vectors, and conditional association is not causation.

Read the lessons in sequence, reproduce a calculation by hand, then run the related Python demonstration and explain which mathematical claim the output illustrates. A numerical observation is never, by itself, proof of a theorem.
